description: What an OS does, kernel vs user space

screens.body:
The operating system is the manager between your programs and the hardware. Your app wants to save a file? It doesn't touch the disk — it asks the OS.

Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS — all operating systems. Without one, every program would need its own drivers for every device. Chaos.

options: Between programs and hardware, managing access
check.question: The OS sits…

screens.heading: What is an OS, really?
screens.keyPoint: The OS manages programs' access to hardware.

screens.body:
The kernel is the heart of the OS — the part that talks to hardware directly. CPU, memory, disk, keyboard: the kernel controls them all.

Everything else (your apps, even parts of the OS like the file explorer) asks the kernel for help instead of touching hardware themselves.

options: Talks to hardware directly; everything else asks it for help
Is a type of app you install
check.question: The kernel…

screens.heading: The kernel: the core
screens.keyPoint: Only the kernel touches hardware directly.

screens.body:
Memory is split into two worlds. User space: where your apps run. Kernel space: where the kernel runs. A wall stands between them.

Why the wall? So a buggy app can't crash the whole system. Your app can crash itself all day; the kernel keeps everything else alive.

options: Protects the system from buggy apps
Slows everything down for no reason
check.question: The wall between user and kernel space…

screens.heading: User space vs kernel space
screens.keyPoint: The wall keeps a buggy app from killing the system.

screens.body:
Apps can't cross the wall freely — but they can knock. A system call is how a program asks the kernel to do something privileged: open a file, send network data, create a process.

When your Node app reads a file, it's making system calls under the hood. Thousands per second, and you never notice.

options: A program asking the kernel to do something privileged
A phone call to tech support
check.question: A system call is…

screens.heading: System calls: the door in the wall
screens.keyPoint: System calls are how apps ask the kernel for help.

screens.body:
CPU, memory, disk space, network, camera, printer — every program wants them, and there's only so much to go around. The OS is the referee.

It decides which program runs on the CPU right now, who gets memory, and who waits. Fairness and order, thousands of decisions per second.

options: Decides who gets CPU, memory, and devices — and when
check.question: Resource management means the OS…

screens.heading: The OS manages resources
screens.keyPoint: The OS is the referee for scarce resources.

screens.body:
You think in files, folders, and windows. The hardware thinks in disk sectors and pixels. The OS translates — those friendly ideas are called abstractions.

Processes, files, and sockets are the big three. They hide enormous complexity so you can just open(), read(), and write().

options: Hides hardware complexity behind a simple idea like 'file'
check.question: An OS abstraction…

screens.heading: Abstractions: simple ideas over messy hardware
screens.keyPoint: Files and processes hide hardware complexity.

screens.body:
Your Learn SD app runs on Vercel's servers — which run Linux. Your Node backend makes system calls every time it reads a file or opens a database connection.

When a deploy fails with "permission denied" or a port is "already in use", that's the OS talking. Understanding it turns scary errors into quick fixes.
screens.heading: Why this matters for you
screens.keyPoint: Deploy errors are often the OS talking.
